summary: Defines a framework for authentication and authorization in Internet of Things settings, based on OAuth 2.0 and CoAP. It turns a widely used authorization approach into a form suitable for small devices, reusing existing specifications where possible and adding extensions and profiles for IoT use cases.

plainLanguage.summary: ACE keeps the part of OAuth that works on any device: the client asks an authorization server for permission, gets a token, and shows the token to the server holding the resource. What changes is the size of everything. The conversation can run over CoAP instead of HTTP, the messages are CBOR instead of JSON, and the token is tied to a key so that a stolen token is useless on its own.

questions: what is a proof of possession token
subtitle: OAuth 2.0 reshaped for tiny devices: CoAP, CBOR and proof-of-possession tokens instead of bearer tokens over HTTPS.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 assumes HTTP over TLS and a JSON body, and it hands the client a bearer token that anyone who sees it can use. Small devices often cannot afford TLS, cannot afford a JSON parser, and cannot keep a secret safely.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9200 keeps the OAuth 2.0 authorization model and replaces the plumbing: CoAP for transport, CBOR for encoding, COSE for securing the token itself, and proof-of-possession tokens that are bound to a key the client must prove it holds. The client also delivers the token once, to an authorization information endpoint on the resource server, instead of with every request.
tldr.outcome: An access token now works only for the client it was issued to, and the framework runs over protocols a small radio can afford. Profiles pin down which transport and security protocol each deployment uses. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9200 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022, and it has not been obsoleted. It defines the ACE framework on top of the OAuth 2.0 model of RFC 6749, and its profiles, such as the DTLS profile in RFC 9202, build on it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Authorization is the process for granting approval to an entity to access a generic resource. The authorization task can best be described as granting access to a requesting client for a resource hosted on a device, the resource server. This exchange is mediated by one or more authorization servers. Managing authorization for a large number of devices and users can be a complex task.

While prior work on authorization solutions for the Web and for the mobile environment also applies to the Internet of Things environment, many IoT devices are constrained, for example in terms of processing capabilities and available memory. For such devices, the Constrained Application Protocol can alleviate some resource concerns when used instead of HTTP to implement the communication flows of this specification.

The specification describes a framework for Authentication and Authorization for Constrained Environments, built on reuse of OAuth 2.0, thereby extending authorization to Internet of Things devices. It contains the building blocks for adjusting OAuth 2.0 to IoT environments.

Profiles of this framework are available in separate specifications, such as RFC 9202 or RFC 9203. A profile may specify the use of the framework for a specific security protocol and the underlying transports for a specific deployment environment, to improve interoperability. Implementations may claim conformance with a specific profile, whereby implementations using the same profile interoperate, while implementations of different profiles are not expected to interoperate. More powerful devices, such as mobile phones and tablets, may implement multiple profiles and will therefore be able to interact with a wider range of constrained devices.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework itself is deliberately not a complete protocol. It sets out the pieces, and a profile says which transport and which security protocol to use with them. Two devices that follow the same profile can talk to each other; two that follow different ones generally cannot.

sections.title: The Building Blocks
sections.content:
The basic block is the OAuth 2.0 framework, which enjoys widespread deployment. Many IoT devices can support OAuth 2.0 without any additional extensions, but for certain constrained settings additional profiling is needed.

Another building block is the lightweight web transfer protocol CoAP, for those communication environments where HTTP is not appropriate. CoAP typically runs on top of UDP, which further reduces overhead and message exchanges. While this specification defines extensions for the use of OAuth over CoAP, other underlying protocols are not prohibited from being supported in the future, such as HTTP/2, MQTT, Bluetooth Low Energy and QUIC.

A third building block is the Concise Binary Object Representation, for encodings where JSON is not sufficiently compact. CBOR is a binary encoding designed for small code and message size. Self-contained tokens and protocol message payloads are encoded in CBOR when CoAP is used, and when CoAP is not used the use of CBOR remains recommended.

A fourth building block is CBOR Object Signing and Encryption, which enables object-level layer security as an alternative or complement to transport layer security such as DTLS or TLS. COSE is used to secure self-contained tokens, such as proof-of-possession tokens, which are an extension to the OAuth bearer tokens. The default token format is defined in CBOR Web Token. Application-layer security for CoAP using COSE can be provided with Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments.

On OAuth 2.0 itself: the framework enables a client to obtain scoped access to a resource with the permission of a resource owner. Access tokens are credentials needed to access protected resources, generated by the authorization server and consumed by the resource server, and their content is opaque to the client. Introspection is a method for a resource server to query the authorization server for the active state and content of a received access token, which is useful when the authorization decisions are very dynamic or when the token is an opaque reference rather than a self-contained token. Refresh tokens are credentials used to obtain new access tokens when the current one expires; unlike access tokens, they are intended for use only with authorization servers and are never sent to resource servers.

CoAP is an application-layer protocol similar to HTTP but specifically designed for constrained environments. It typically uses datagram-oriented transport, such as UDP, where reordering and loss of packets can occur. While HTTP uses headers and query strings to convey additional information about a request, CoAP encodes such information into header parameters called options. CoAP supports application-layer fragmentation of payloads through block-wise transfers, but block-wise transfer does not increase the size limits of CoAP options, so data encoded in options has to be kept small.
sections.plainLanguage: Four pieces are reused rather than reinvented: OAuth for the authorization model, CoAP for talking to small devices, CBOR for a compact binary format, and COSE for signing and encrypting the token itself. The point of using them is that they are already written and already fit small devices.

sections.title: Protocol Interactions
sections.content:
The framework is based on the OAuth 2.0 protocol interactions using the token endpoint and optionally the introspection endpoint. A client obtains an access token, and optionally a refresh token, from an authorization server using the token endpoint, and subsequently presents the access token to a resource server to gain access to a protected resource. In most deployments the resource server can process the access token locally, but in some cases it may present it to the authorization server via the introspection endpoint to get fresh information.

Requesting an access token. The client makes an access token request to the token endpoint at the authorization server. The framework assumes the use of proof-of-possession access tokens, in which the authorization server binds a key to an access token. The client may include the permissions it seeks to obtain and information about the credentials it wants to use for proof of possession, such as whether to use symmetric or asymmetric cryptography, or a reference to a specific key.

Access token response. If the request has been successfully verified, authenticated and authorized, the authorization server returns an access token and optionally a refresh token. Only certain grant types support refresh tokens. The server can also return additional parameters referred to as Access Information, which the framework defines to inform the client about the capabilities of the resource server, for example the profile the resource server supports.

Resource request. The client interacts with the resource server to request access to the protected resource and provides the access token. The protocol used between the client and the resource server is not restricted to CoAP; HTTP, HTTP/2, QUIC, MQTT and Bluetooth Low Energy are also viable. Depending on the device limitations and the selected protocol, this exchange may be split in two: the client sends the access token, containing or referencing the authorization information, to the resource server, and then the client makes the resource access request using the communication security protocol and the other Access Information obtained from the authorization server. The client and the resource server mutually authenticate using the security protocol specified in the profile and the keys obtained in the access token or the Access Information. The resource server verifies that the token is integrity protected and originated by the authorization server, and then compares the claims contained in the token with the resource request. If the resource server is online, validation can be handed over to the authorization server using token introspection.

Token introspection. A resource server may be configured to introspect the access token by including it in a request to the introspection endpoint at that authorization server. Introspection is an optional step and can be omitted if the token is self-contained and the resource server is prepared to perform the token validation on its own. The authorization server validates the token and returns the most recent parameters, such as scope, audience and validity, and the resource server uses them to accept or deny the request.

Protected resource. If the request is authorized, the resource server fulfills it and returns a response with the appropriate response code, using the dynamically established keys to protect the response according to the communication security protocol used.
sections.plainLanguage: Six steps. The client asks the authorization server for a token. The server gives one, and may also tell the client which security protocol to use. The client hands the token to the resource server once, then makes its actual request. If the server wants to check the token with the authorization server, it introspects it. The server then answers the request, protected with keys it has established.

sections.title: The Framework
sections.content:
Credential provisioning. In constrained environments it cannot be assumed that the client and the resource server are part of a common key infrastructure. The authorization server therefore provisions credentials and associated information to allow mutual authentication between the client and the resource server, and the resulting security association may then also be used to bind these credentials to the access tokens the client uses.

Proof of possession. The framework implements proof of possession for access tokens by default, that is, that the token holder can prove being a holder of the key bound to the token. The binding is provided by the cnf, confirmation, claim, indicating what key is used. If a client needs to submit a new access token, for example to obtain additional access rights, it can request that the authorization server binds it to the same key as the previous one.

Profiles. The client or resource server may be limited in the encodings or protocols it supports, so specific interactions between the client and the resource server are defined in a profile. The authorization server is expected to manage the matching of compatible profile choices between a client and a resource server, and informs the client of the selected profile using the ace_profile parameter in the token response.

OAuth 2.0 requires TLS to protect the communication between the authorization server and client, between the client and the resource server when accessing a resource, and between the authorization server and the resource server if introspection is used. In constrained settings TLS is not always feasible or desirable, but it is required that those communications are encrypted, integrity protected and protected against message replay, and that the communicating endpoints perform mutual authentication. It must also be assured that responses are bound to requests, so that the receiver of a response can be certain that it belongs to a particular request. Setting up such a secure communication may require some unprotected messages to be exchanged first, such as sending the token from the client to the resource server.

When profiles use CoAP instead of HTTP, it is required to use a CBOR map as the payload of the POST request instead of URI-query parameters, and the CBOR encoding for the OAuth parameters is specified in the document. Profiles that use CBOR encoding at the outermost encoding layer must use the Content-Format application/ace+cbor, abbreviated with the ID 19 if CoAP is used. The OAuth 2.0 authorization server uses a JSON structure in the payload of its responses, and if CoAP is used it is required to use CBOR instead of JSON.

Discovering authorization servers. The client must discover the authorization server in charge of the resource server, both to find out the URI to which the token request must be sent and to validate that the authorization server with that URI is authorized to provide access tokens for that resource server. To find the URI the client may send an initial Unauthorized Resource Request to the resource server, which denies the request and sends the address of its authorization server back. How the client validates that authorization is out of scope, and may involve asking the owner or querying a dedicated secure service provided by the client owner.

Unauthorized Resource Request. A resource server must treat any request for a protected resource as an Unauthorized Resource Request when the request arrived on an unsecured channel, when it has no valid access token for the sender regarding the requested action, or when it has a valid token that does not authorize the requested action. These conditions let the resource server handle requests autonomously once access has been granted and a secure channel exists. The authz-info endpoint is not itself a protected resource and must not be protected in this way. Unauthorized Resource Request messages must be denied with an unauthorized_client error response, in which the resource server should provide AS Request Creation Hints so the client can request an access token from the right place. Those hints are a CBOR or JSON map with an optional AS element giving an absolute URI, and optional elements for the audience the client should request, the key identifier of a key, and the profile to use.
sections.plainLanguage: Three design rules run through the framework. The token is bound to a key the client must prove it holds, so a stolen token does not work. The client and the resource server need credentials, and the authorization server hands them out. And the client must be able to check that the response it got belongs to the request it sent, so that an old answer cannot be replayed at it.

sections.title: The Access Token and the Authorization Information Endpoint
sections.content:
The use of CBOR Web Token is recommended. To facilitate offline processing of access tokens, the document uses the cnf claim and the scope claim for JWT- and CWT-encoded tokens, and a binary encoding of the scope may be used. If the authorization server needs to hint to the resource server about which profile to use with the client, it may include an ace_profile claim in the access token. If the client submitted a cnonce parameter in the access token request, the authorization server must include that value in the cnonce claim, which uses binary encoding.

The authorization information endpoint. The access token, carrying the authorization information and the information about the proof-of-possession method, has to be transported to the resource server so that it can authenticate and authorize the client request. The method consists of an authz-info endpoint implemented by the resource server. A client using it must make a POST request to that endpoint with the access token in the payload, and the content format or media type must reflect the format of the token, for example application/cwt for CBOR Web Tokens, or application/octet-stream when no format is defined. The resource server must verify the validity of the token, and if it is valid must respond with a response code equivalent to CoAP code 2.01, Created. The resource server must be prepared to store at least one access token for future use, which is a difference from OAuth 2.0 where the access token is typically sent with each request and therefore not stored. It is recommended that a resource server stores only one token per proof-of-possession key, so that an additional token linked to the same key supersedes any existing one; this greatly simplifies constrained implementations with respect to storage and to resolving a request to the applicable token. If the payload does not parse to a token, the resource server must respond with CoAP code 4.00, Bad Request. The resource server may make an introspection request to validate the token before responding, for example when the token is an opaque reference. Profiles must specify whether the authz-info endpoint is protected, including whether error responses are protected, since the token contains the information that lets the client and the resource server establish a security context in the first place, mutual authentication may not be possible at that point. The default name of this endpoint in a URL path is /authz-info, but implementations are not required to use it.

Verifying an access token. When a resource server receives an access token it must verify it before storing it. The details depend on the token encoding, since the security protection differs: a CWT uses COSE while a JWT uses JOSE. The type of token also matters, since a self-contained token can be verified locally while a reference token requires interaction with the authorization server. Self-contained tokens must at least be integrity protected and may also be encrypted. For a self-contained token the resource server must process the security protection first, which must include verifying that the token was generated by an authorization server that has the right to issue access tokens for that resource server.

Errors during this initial processing are handled in defined ways. If verification of the security wrapper fails, or the token was issued by an authorization server without the right to issue tokens for the receiving resource server, the token is discarded and the response is CoAP code 4.01, Unauthorized. If the claims cannot be obtained, the token is discarded and the response is CoAP code 4.00, Bad Request.

The claims are then verified, in a stated order of priority. The iss claim, if present, must identify the authorization server that produced the security protection, or the token is discarded and the response is CoAP 4.01. The exp claim's expiration date must be in the future, or the token is discarded and the response is CoAP 4.01, and the resource server has to terminate access rights when tokens expire. The aud claim must refer to an audience the resource server identifies with, or the token is discarded and the response is CoAP 4.03, Forbidden. The resource server must recognise the value of the scope claim, or the token is discarded and the response is CoAP 4.00, Bad Request.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sending the token with every request, the client posts it once to the resource server, which checks it and keeps it. The checks run in a fixed order: who issued it, has it expired, is it meant for this server, and does the client have the right scope. Each failure has its own status code, so the client can tell a bad token from an expired one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations applicable to authentication and authorization in RESTful environments provided in OAuth 2.0 apply, as do the additional considerations for OAuth in RFC 6819 and, if the introspection endpoint is used, those of RFC 7662.

Protecting tokens. A large range of threats can be mitigated by protecting the contents of the access token with a digital signature or a keyed message digest, so the token integrity protection must be applied, particularly since the token contains a reference to the key used for proof of possession. If the access token contains the symmetric key, that key must be encrypted by the authorization server so that only the resource server can decrypt it. Using an AEAD algorithm is preferable to using a MAC unless the token needs to be publicly readable. If the token is intended for multiple recipients, integrity protection with a symmetric key shared between the authorization server and the recipients is not sufficient, since any recipient could modify the token undetected by the others, so a token with a multirecipient audience must be protected with an asymmetric signature. It is important for the authorization server to include the identity of the intended recipient in the token, and the same shared secret must not be used as a proof-of-possession key with multiple resource servers. If clients are capable of doing so they should frequently request fresh access tokens, which allows shorter token lifetimes and therefore shorter proof-of-possession keys. When authorization servers bind symmetric keys to access tokens, they should scope these tokens to a specific permission.

Communication security. Communication with the authorization server must use confidentiality protection, because the client or the resource server may obtain the proof-of-possession key there for use with a specific access token; without confidentiality that secret is exposed to an eavesdropper, completely negating proof-of-possession security. Additional protection can be applied by encrypting the token, for example encryption of CWTs, which may be necessary if the token is later transferred over an insecure connection such as the authz-info endpoint. Care must be taken to prevent leakage of the proof-of-possession credentials, because an adversary in possession of them can impersonate the client. This is a real risk in many constrained environments, since adversaries may get physical access to devices and use physical extraction techniques to reach memory contents; it can be mitigated by refreshing keys frequently, by software isolation, and by hardware security.

Long-term credentials. Both clients and resource servers have long-term credentials used to secure communications and authenticate to the authorization server, and these need protection against unauthorized access, which can be difficult in constrained devices deployed in publicly accessible places without specialized hardware such as secure key storage. The loss of a credential linked to a specific device must not lead to a compromise of other credentials not linked to that device, so secret keys used for authentication must not be shared between more than two parties. Operators should have procedures to replace credentials that are suspected to be compromised or lost, and to securely erase credentials when decommissioning devices.

Unprotected hints. Initially no secure channel exists between the client and the resource server, so the client cannot tell whether the hints in an unprotected response are authentic. The client must therefore determine whether an authorization server is authorized to provide access tokens for a given resource server.

Minimal requirements for communication. All communication between the client and the authorization server must be encrypted and integrity and replay protected, and responses from the authorization server must be bound to the client's request to avoid an attacker swapping the intended response for an older one valid for a previous request. Communication between the resource server and the authorization server via the introspection endpoint must be encrypted and integrity and replay protected, with responses bound to the request. The initial communication between the client and the resource server cannot be secured in general, because the resource server does not yet hold an access token for that client, but if both parties support DTLS without client authentication it is recommended to use it to protect that initial communication. After the client has successfully transmitted the access token, a secure communication protocol must be established between the client and the resource server for the actual resource request, providing confidentiality, integrity, replay protection, and a binding between requests and responses.

Token freshness and expiration. A resource server that is offline faces the problem of clock drift: since it cannot synchronize its clock with the authorization server, it may be tricked into accepting old access tokens that are no longer valid or have been compromised. It may use the nonce-based mechanism to ensure freshness. Another problem with clock drift is that evaluating the standard expiration claim can give unpredictable results. The expiration mechanism implemented by the expires-in claim, based on the first time the resource server sees the token, was defined to provide a more predictable alternative, but it has drawbacks: a malicious client may hold back tokens with that claim to prolong their lifespan, and a resource server that loses state may lose the counters tracking them, which can be mitigated by regularly storing the counter values to persistent memory.

Unprotected information. Communication with the authz-info endpoint and the error responses potentially sends information over an unprotected channel, which may leak information to an adversary or be manipulated by active attackers. Error responses for requests to the authorization information endpoint can reveal information about an otherwise opaque access token to an adversary who has intercepted the token. The framework is written on the assumption that the benefits of detailed error messages outweigh the risk of information leakage, and for use cases where that assessment does not apply, detailed error messages can be replaced by more generic ones. Where the authz-info endpoint cannot be protected, it is recommended to use encrypted CWTs or tokens that are opaque references and need introspection. If the initial Unauthorized Resource Request is used, the client must make sure it is not sending sensitive content, since GET and DELETE requests only reveal the target URI while POST and PUT would reveal the whole payload of the intended operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules carry most of the weight. The key bound to a token must never travel in the clear, or the whole point of the token is lost. And the channel to the resource server cannot be protected until the client has handed over the token, so the first message is the one that is exposed. The document says to keep the token itself encrypted so that the exposed message says as little as possible.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Implementers and users should be aware of the privacy implications of the different possible deployments of this framework. The authorization server is in a very central position and can potentially learn sensitive information about the clients requesting access tokens. If the client credentials grant is used, the authorization server can track what kind of access the client intends to perform; with other grants this can be prevented by the resource owner, who needs to bind the grants it issues to anonymous, ephemeral credentials that do not allow the authorization server to link different grants, and thus different access token requests by the same client.

The claims contained in a token can reveal privacy-sensitive information about the client and the resource server to any party having access to them, whether by processing the content of a self-contained token or by introspection. The authorization server should be configured to minimize the information about clients and resource servers disclosed in the tokens it issues. If tokens are only integrity protected and not encrypted, they may reveal information to attackers listening on the wire, and in the case of CBOR Web Tokens the token may reveal the audience, the scope, and the confirmation method used by the client; the latter may reveal the identity of the device or application running the client, which may be linkable to the identity of the person using it.

Clients using asymmetric keys for proof of possession should be aware of the consequences of using the same key pair towards different resource servers: a set of colluding resource servers, or an attacker able to obtain the access tokens, will be able to link the requests or even determine the client's identity.

An unprotected response to an unauthorized request may disclose information about the resource server and its existing relationship with the client. It is advisable to include as little information as possible in an unencrypted response, since even the absolute URI of the authorization server may reveal sensitive information about the service the resource server provides. Developers must ensure that the resource server does not disclose information that has an impact on the privacy of the stakeholders in the AS Request Creation Hints.
sections.plainLanguage: The authorization server sees a lot, and the token itself can leak. If the token is only signed and not encrypted, anyone who can read it learns the audience, the scope, and which key the client used, which may identify the device and through it the person using it. The document asks for tokens to carry as little as possible and to be encrypted where they might be overheard.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document creates several registries with a registration policy of Expert Review: the ACE Authorization Server Request Creation Hints registry, the CoRE Resource Types, OAuth Extensions Errors, OAuth Error Code CBOR Mappings, OAuth Grant Type CBOR Mappings, OAuth Access Token Types, OAuth Access Token Type CBOR Mappings, ACE Profiles, OAuth Parameters, OAuth Parameters CBOR Mappings, OAuth Introspection Response Parameters, OAuth Token Introspection Response CBOR Mappings, JSON Web Token Claims, CBOR Web Token Claims, and the CoAP Content-Formats.

A new token type is registered in the OAuth Access Token Types registry with the name PoP, with the additional token endpoint response parameters cnf and rs_cnf, no HTTP authentication scheme, the IETF as change controller, and this document as the reference.

The media type application/ace+cbor is registered for messages of the protocols defined in the document carrying parameters encoded in CBOR. It must be encoded as a CBOR map containing the protocol parameters defined in RFC 9200, and the security considerations are those of Section 6 of that document.
sections.plainLanguage: A new token type called PoP is registered, a media type for CBOR-encoded messages is registered, and a set of registries is created so that new parameters, claims and profiles can be added later under review.

viz.caption: The four building blocks of the ACE framework

items.title: OAuth 2.0
items.text: The authorization model: a client gets a scoped access token from an authorization server and presents it to a resource server.

items.title: CoAP
items.text: A lightweight request and response protocol for constrained networks, usually over UDP, with request information carried in options.

items.title: CBOR
items.text: A compact binary encoding used instead of JSON for protocol parameters and for the token itself.

items.title: COSE
items.text: Object-level signing and encryption, used to protect self-contained proof-of-possession tokens.
